page4_img_1.png.title: Data model: requirements/issues linked to commits via LDA topics
page4_img_1.png.description: A schematic three-column diagram showing Requirements or Issue Reports (left) mapped into one or more central Topic nodes, which in turn connect to multiple Commit targets (right). The bi-directional arrow structure implies many-to-many relationships: several documents contribute to a topic, and a single topic can be associated with many commits (and commits can relate to multiple topics). This visual encodes the paper’s processing pipeline: LDA extracts topic word-distributions from requirements/issues and then LDA inference is used to relate commits to those pre-existing topics, producing the topic–document associations the authors use for time-series topic-plots.

page30_img_1.png.title: Comparison of expert vs non-expert labels for selected LDA topics
page30_img_1.png.description: A cropped table (Table 2) showing five sampled requirement topics (Topic 1, 5, 6, 15, 18) with their top-ranked LDA words, a non-expert (author) label and several expert-provided labels/notes for each topic. The top-word lists contain many domain tokens and redactions (shown as long dashes) — for example Topic 1 includes words like "state thread return connection call wininet...dns typedef" and the non-expert suggested "wifi code?", while experts interpreted it as connectivity/connection-sharing or network-related work. Topic 5’s words (e.g., "network connect wifi hotspot connection probe...authentication reconnect") led both non-expert and experts to identify wifi/hotspot or network service concerns; Topic 6 and 18 were similarly read as setup/certificates and RIL/setup-related configuration respectively. Topic 15, however, shows experts repeatedly marking it "Not coherent" or generic (connectivity/testing), illustrating that some LDA topics were hard for practitioners to interpret or lacked cohesive semantics.

page19_img_table_1.png.title: Table of FLOSS projects with issue and commit counts
page19_img_table_1.png.description: A three-column table listing each FLOSS participant’s project (name, URL and brief description) alongside two numeric columns: Issues and Commits. The table summarizes 13 projects used in the study and shows wide variation in activity — issue counts range from single digits up to 242 and commit counts range from about 52 to roughly 2,700 (for example, one project shows 242 issues and ~2,714 commits while another shows 14 issues and 52 commits). The table is captioned “FLOSS Developers and their Projects” and was used to report which projects and activity volumes were included in the FLOSS replication of the study.

page31_img_1.png.title: Callout: 50% agreement between expert and non-expert topic labels
page31_img_1.png.description: A wide horizontal callout box containing a single centered sentence in large serif type: "Only 50% of expertly labelled topic labels were similar or agreed with the non-expert topic labels." The paper reports this figure corresponds to 23 matches out of 46 industrial labellings, and elsewhere notes an average per-topic agreement of about 40% between non-expert and expert labels. The statistic is presented as a takeaway highlighting why the authors recommend using domain experts to label LDA-extracted topics.

page26_img_1.png.title: Callout: 46–48% agreement that topic-plots matched developers' perceptions
page26_img_1.png.description: A framed quotation box summarizing a survey result: respondents reported that the presented topic-plot matched their perception of the effort for that topic, with 46–48% of topic-plot ratings agreeing for both industrial and FLOSS developers. The graphic uses large, centered serif text and horizontal rules to highlight this takeaway and references Figure 8 for the detailed rating distribution. It serves as a succinct, visual summary of the moderate agreement across participant groups about the validity of the topic-plot visualization.

page33_img_1.png.title: Agreement between non-expert and expert topic labels (20 topics)
page33_img_1.png.description: Stacked bar chart showing, for Microsoft Topics 1–20 on the x‑axis, the count of expert labelings that either matched (dark bars) or mismatched (light bars) the non‑expert labels; numeric annotations on each bar show the exact counts. The plot highlights wide variability in agreement across topics (some topics have several matches, others more mismatches), with Topic 19 standing out as the largest pure agreement case (five matches, no mismatches) and Topic 6 among those with many mismatches. Several topics received few or no labels, indicating limited overlap in expert responses for those topics. This visual supports the paper’s report that non‑expert labels only agreed with expert labels on the order of about 40% on average, motivating the recommendation to use domain experts for labelling.

page23_img_1.png.title: Multi-project FLOSS issue-topic time-series (commit relevance)
page23_img_1.png.description: A multi-panel collage of area/time-series plots showing, for many FLOSS projects, the average per-time-window relevance of commits to individual LDA-extracted issue topics. Each subplot is titled with the project and a topic number plus the top-ranked topic words (the LDA word lists), the X axis is time and the Y axis is average commit relevance (larger = more relevant). Red dashed vertical lines mark project releases or milestones; panels display varied behavior (some topics show sharp spikes near releases, others show sustained or intermittent activity) that was presented to developers during the survey to validate whether these topic-relevance trends matched their perception of work on those topics.

page27_img_1.png.title: Stacked bar of topic‑plot perceptual ratings by Microsoft and FLOSS developers
page27_img_1.png.description: Stacked bar chart comparing how Microsoft (light gray) and FLOSS (dark gray) developers rated whether topic‑plots matched their perception of effort across six response categories (NA, Strongly Disagree, Disagree, Neutral, Agree, Strongly Agree). Microsoft counts: NA=3, Strongly Disagree=3, Disagree=4, Neutral=3, Agree=10, Strongly Agree=1. FLOSS counts: NA=0, Strongly Disagree=1, Disagree=8, Neutral=10, Agree=15, Strongly Agree=3. Combined totals show most responses in "Agree" (25) followed by "Neutral" (13) and "Disagree" (12); the paper reports these distributions were not statistically different between the two groups.

page21_img_1.png.title: Personal topic-plots for two developers showing topic relevance over time
page21_img_1.png.description: Two columns show personal topic-plots for two different developers; each column contains two stacked area charts (top: purple, bottom: red) plotting average commit relevance to a topic over time. The x-axis spans roughly May 2005 to June 2011 and the y-axis is labeled “average commit relevance.” The top charts are labeled with the non-expert topic words “use cases features: what's GAT? is this just a cross-general topic of common terms?” and the bottom charts with “------- testing and power?”; each chart exhibits different temporal peaks and plateaus (for example, the top-right plot shows a large sustained peak around 2007–2008 while the top-left plot has more intermittent peaks earlier and around 2009), illustrating that different developers' focus on the same kinds of topics evolves differently over the project lifetime.

page21_img_2.png.title: Team topic-plots for ‘testing/metrics/milestones’ and ‘music player’ (2002–2011)
page21_img_2.png.description: A 2×2 panel of area charts showing average commit relevance over time (x-axis: 2002/05/21–2011/06/08; y-axis labeled “average commit relevance”). Each column represents a different team, and each column contains two topic-plots: the top row is labeled “testing, metrics and milestones: is this process?” (filled in teal) and the bottom row is labeled “music player: volume, song, controls and ------- controls?” (filled in magenta). The testing/metrics topic shows substantial activity early in the timeline with multiple peaks around 2004–2006 and a long decline to near-zero relevance after ~2007, while the music-player topic has low baseline relevance with intermittent spikes (notably series of peaks in later years on the left panel and a sharp mid‑2006 spike on the right), indicating that the testing topic dominated earlier development effort whereas music-player work appeared more sporadically and later. A thin black line overlays each area as a trend/smoothing of the relevance series.

page29_img_1.png.title: Refheap Topic 4 — average commit relevance over time
page29_img_1.png.description: Area chart titled with the top LDA words for Topic 4 (truncated in the title) plotting Avg. Commit Relevance (y-axis, 0–0.7) against Time (x-axis, Jan 2012 to Jan 2013). The yellow filled area shows intermittent spikes in topic-relevant commits: the largest peak is about 0.7 in mid‑May 2012, a secondary peak near 0.3–0.35 in late June 2012, two smaller spikes (~0.2–0.3) around November 2012 that coincide with two red dashed vertical lines marking releases/milestones, and a renewed rise around January 2013 (~0.35). A thin trend line slightly declines across the period, indicating a small overall decrease in average relevance; the topic label (top words shown in the title) led developers to associate this topic with UI/keyboard‑shortcut/highlighting work (e.g., jquery.hotkeys).

page14_img_1.png.title: Personal topic-plot of developer showing commit relevance to Topic 13 over time
page14_img_1.png.description: A time-series plot of average commit relevance for an LDA-derived topic (labelled at top with top words: “Topic 13 component set policy context service mode high …”) from 2010-04-15 to 2011-06-23. The x-axis is time (date ticks shown from April 2010 to June 2011) and the y-axis is Avg. Commit Relevance (bins of equal time; the per-bin relevance is the average of commit–topic relevance values, set to 0 when no commits occur). The series is near zero for the first months, shows small isolated spikes in mid/2010 and larger, repeated peaks from late 2010 into early/mid 2011 (the largest peak reaches roughly 2.5 on the y-axis), indicating several concentrated bursts of this developer’s topic-relevant commits. This figure is the personal view for one industrial developer and uses the authors’ non-expert topic label to help interpret the plotted behaviour.

page24_img_1.png.title: Collage of FLOSS issue-topic time-series with release markers
page24_img_1.png.description: A multi-panel collage of issue‑tracker topic‑plots (LDA topics) for several FLOSS projects (panel headings include project names such as Craft.NET, DNDS, ASPEN, Aura, Kindlebility, and Form‑Sensible‑Reflector‑DBIC). Each small panel is an area chart showing average topic relevance on the Y axis over time on the X axis, with the topic’s top-ranked words printed as the panel label; red dashed vertical lines mark project releases or milestones. Panels illustrate different temporal behaviors — isolated spikes, clusters of short bursts around releases, and long plateaus of activity — that the authors used to ask developers whether the plotted effort matched their recollection. These plots were presented in the FLOSS survey so respondents could label topics and judge whether peaks or trends corresponded to real development or release events.

page9_img_1.png.title: Craft.NET issue-topic small-multiples showing average commit relevance over time
page9_img_1.png.description: A 20-panel small-multiples figure (one panel per LDA topic) plotting average commit relevance over time for the Craft.NET project, with the x‑axis spanning roughly July 2012 to January 2013 and the y‑axis labelled “Avg. Commit Relevance.” Each panel is titled “Topic N” followed by the top-ranked LDA words (the paper’s representation of topic content), and vertical red dashed lines mark releases or milestones. Panels show varied temporal patterns: several topics (for example Topic 1, Topic 3, Topic 6, Topic 9, Topic 13, Topic 19 and Topic 20) exhibit pronounced spikes of relevance indicating concentrated commit activity, whereas other topics remain low or diffuse across the interval. The differing peak heights between panels (some panels reach values >1–2 while others stay below 0.5) indicate that the magnitude and timing of issue-related work vary substantially by topic, and some spikes appear near the red release lines suggesting clustered effort around milestones.

page8_img_1.png.title: Requirements topic-plots showing topic relevance (2000–2010)
page8_img_1.png.description: A 4×5 grid of 20 small time-series panels, each plotting a single LDA-derived requirements topic’s average relevance (filled colored area) across equal-length time bins from mid‑2000 to mid‑2010 (x-axis), with the y-axis showing average relevance per bin (larger = more relevant). Each panel is labelled with the authors’ non‑expert topic label (some tokens redacted with long dashes) and shows distinct behaviors — e.g., narrow early spikes (the “wifi code?” topic peaks around 2002), long-term rises (one topic shows almost no activity for the first seven years then a sustained increase later in the decade), and declines for testing/use‑case topics. The plots were used to link requirements topics to commits over time; the paper notes specific spikes (topics 7 and 9) that a program manager associated with Design Change Requests such as Bluetooth work, illustrating how these topic‑plots can surface real development events and changing effort focus.

page32_img_table_1.png.title: FLOSS developers’ per-project issue-topic words with developer labels/comments
page32_img_table_1.png.description: This table presents one issue-tracker LDA topic per FLOSS project as given to the surveyed developers: for each row it shows (an anonymized) developer, the project name, the topic identifier, the top-ranked topic words produced by LDA, and the developer’s written interpretation or label. There are 13 rows (one per responding developer/project) and each developer comment directly follows the list of topic words. Representative responses: one developer called the topic words “nonsensical” for their audio‑book reader project, another linked words to Makefile/distribution changes, a third interpreted terms as Windows installation/library issues, and several noted spurious tokens (usernames or punctuation) that made labeling harder. Overall the entries illustrate a mix of useful mappings to concrete features or build tasks and frequent complaints about noise or ambiguity in raw LDA word lists.
